dream_response:
The cedar is warm enough to seep through the thin cotton of my shirt cuff, dry and resin-thick, the faint tang of it mixing with the tacky fake-cherry popsicle residue smudged under my wrist—left from the popsicle I ate 20 minutes ago, the kind that stains the pads of your fingers neon pink, that leaves a sweet-tart tang on your tongue even after the last bite is gone. There’s a splinter, tiny, pale, pricking the soft inside of my wrist just enough to register, not enough to hurt, not enough to make me bother picking it out. Moving would break the slow, anyway.

A dandelion puff tears loose from its stem three feet out, bobbing so slow in the thin breeze it looks suspended, catching the honeyed light so each tiny parachute glows like spun glass. It drifts down to land on the ear of the matted orange tabby I didn’t notice curled on the lowest porch step, burrs stuck in its flank, paws tucked under its chin. The cat twitches one ear, doesn’t open its eyes, lets out a purr so deep and rumbly it travels up the porch boards, faint as a thrum. One of those overstuffed bumblebees blunders straight into a clover head hard enough to shake loose a bead of honeydew, which plops dead-center on the toe of my scuffed white canvas sneaker, leaving a dark little splotch I don’t bother wiping. The bee doesn’t even act fazed, just crawls drunkenly over the clover blooms, pollen dusting its fuzzy back so thick it looks dusted in turmeric, before bumbling into the next head like it hasn’t got a flight path to follow, no hive quota to meet, nowhere urgent to be.

The screen door two hollows over twangs that familiar warped twang, and after it comes the soft, rough voice of an old woman, not yelling, just calling loud enough for the breeze to carry: “Supper in ten!” Her voice warbles a little, tangled with the sharp-sweet tang of blackberry bloom from the fencerow, with the thin acrid whiff of charcoal starter that’s now softening into the smell of smoldering hickory, of hot dog fat dripping down onto coals, of baked beans thick with molasses and bacon fat drifting up from the grill a quarter mile down. The kid who laughed so hard they snort-yelled earlier yells something back, words too muffled by distance to parse, just the bright, wild edge of it, like they’re running full tilt through the roadside grass, bare feet slapping the packed dirt, chasing the leopard frog they found down in the creek an hour ago. A farm dog barks, not sharp, not protective, just excited, thumping its tail so hard against the side of a porch I can almost hear the soft thud-thud-thud under the grass rustle.

The Carolina wren doesn’t startle when I shift my weight a hair. It tilts its striped head, beady black eye glinting, then dart-hops to the chipped ceramic plate at my elbow, snags the largest crumb of shortcake off the edge—crumb dusted with powdered sugar, smudged with melted whipped cream—then flits back two inches like it’s waiting for me to scold it. I don’t. It cocks its head again, lets out a sharp, trilling chirp that sounds like a tiny, cheeky thank you, then tucks the crumb into a crack in the porch post, right where I can see the edge of its nest peeking out, woven with grass and twine and tufts of orange tabby fur it’s been stealing off the napping cat for weeks. The cat hasn’t noticed. Doesn’t care.

A stray breeze curls cool enough to prickle the back of my neck, carrying with it the faint, slow crunch of gravel under old pickup tires, coming up the hollow so slow it’s barely moving. The driver lifts a sun-crinkled hand out the open window to wave, even though I don’t know his name, and I lift one lazy finger back, don’t even sit up straighter. The truck radio is turned down so low I can just catch the warble of a 70s country track, something about hound dogs and sweet tea, fading as it rounds the bend, leaving a faint whiff of exhaust tangled with pine resin, thin enough not to be annoying, just there. One of the oak’s tassel-like catkins drifts down, lands in my hair, and I don’t pluck it out. The oak’s shadow has crept past my ankle now, inching up my calf, cool against my bare skin where my jeans are rolled up.
There’s a tiny black ant meandering across the tacky popsicle spot on the rail, moving so slow it looks like it’s drunk on sugar, pausing every half second to tap its antennae, no frantic march back to the hill, no rush. It crawls right over the faint, worn lopsided heart carved into the cedar 40-some years ago, initials J+M worn smooth by decades of sun and rain and popsicle spills and sweet tea rings, so faded you can barely make out the letters. A tiny cross spider, no bigger than my pinky nail, has strung a web between the rail and the post right by my elbow, strands strung with dandelion fluff and pollen dust, glowing gold in the low light. It sits dead-center in the web, not moving, waiting for whatever bug drifts by, no hurry to wrap anything up, no deadline to meet.

The mason jar of sweet tea at my elbow sweats slow, beads of condensation running down its fogged sides to darken the cedar under it, leaving a wet ring right over the M in the carved heart. There’s a sprig of mint crushed in the bottom, sugar crusted thick on the rim, ice clinking soft when the breeze hits it, but I don’t reach for it. Not yet. No rush. I brush a finger against the lamb’s ear growing in the step crack, soft as kitten fur, silver-green fuzz catching the light, and a little spring azure butterfly flutters off its bloom, wings so thin the sun shines right through them, to land on the rim of the shortcake plate, bobbing slow around the smudge of melted whipped cream.
The wren comes back for a second crumb, bolder this time, hopping so close I can see the tiny barbs on its feathers, the way its little feet scrabble for purchase on the weathered wood. One of the bumblebees lands on the rail right next to my hand for three whole seconds, buzzing so soft it makes the wood hum under my palm, pollen dusting its legs so thick it looks like it’s wearing little yellow boots, before it lurches off again, straight into a blackberry bloom like it forgot where it was going.
The light is softer now, gilding the edges of the hazy blue ridges, bleeding pale pink into the sky way out over the hollow. The woodpecker that’s been tapping slow up the ridge isn’t drumming to mark territory, just lazy tap-tap… tap, like it’s half-asleep too, pecking at a bug it doesn’t even care that much about catching. In another hour the fireflies will start blinking low in the clover, someone will drag out a chipped mason jar with holes poked in the lid, the mosquitoes will start nipping at my elbows, someone will holler for me to come get a hot dog before they’re all gone. But not right now.
Right now the cat purrs. The wren chirps. The ant crawls slow across the sticky rail. The shadow creeps up my leg, soft as a hand. The air smells like cedar and blackberry bloom and charred hot dog and clover, warm on my cheeks, cool on my neck, no sound louder than the grass rustle, the distant laugh, the soft thrum of the bee. There’s nothing to fix, nothing to say, nothing to make, nothing to prove. The seconds don’t feel like they’re rushing. They just drift, slow as dandelion puffs, soft as lamb’s ear, gold as the light slanting through the oak leaves. I don’t move. I stay. There’s nowhere better to be.

Past the bakery, the little free library mounted on a splintered cedar post leans a little left, door propped open with a smooth river rock. Tucked between a waterlogged romance novel and a beat-up bird field guide, the tattered 1972 coastal navigation manual—cover held on with yellowed packing tape, spine creased so deep pages fall open to the tide pool chapter on their own—hums a sea shanty so soft you have to lean within a foot of the shelf to catch it, something about silver herring runs and thick wool socks and rum-spiked tea warm enough to thaw cold knuckles. A kid stuck a holographic unicorn sticker on its spine last month, and now the shanty carries a tiny, tinkly bell harmony it didn’t have before; no one has left a note complaining.
At the corner, the popsicle cart’s striped awning drips leftover rain in fat slow drops, wild blackberry popsicles stacked in the freezer so cold they frost the clear plastic lid. Three kids perch on the curb, popsicles dripping thick purple juice down their wrists to pool in knuckle creases, staining skin the color of ripe elderberries, and two retired garden gnomes sit cross-legged next to them—pointy red hats faded to soft rose, one with a chip out of his left ear from a 2019 lawnmower incident—showing them how to tie shoelace knots that never come undone. The knots sprout tiny closed daisy buds along the loops if you squint, and one kid’s neon pink shoelace glows so faintly you’d miss it if the sun wasn’t slanting low, bright enough to help them find their sneakers when they kick them off under the porch after dark.

When the last lingering drip from the oak overhead hits the waxy blue chalk of the puppy’s nose, a puff of cinnamon scent curls up, light enough you might write it off as someone baking oatmeal cookies two blocks over, and a house sparrow hops across the drawing, leaving three-toed prints that look like tiny lopsided hearts in the chalk dust.
Up on the porch rails of the pale yellow house, half-empty glasses of sweet iced tea sweat rings into weathered pine, condensation dripping slow to water the potted mint trailing over the edge. Fireflies are out early, roused by the cool rain, their glows dimmer than they’ll be at full dark, plinking soft against the glass sides like tiny clumsy party guests who showed up before the lights went down. One slips on a bead of condensation, tumbles into the tea with a tiny plink, bobs there glowing gold for three seconds before a kid leaning over the rail scoops it out with a popsicle stick, sets it on the rail to dry its gossamer wings; it leaves a faint glowing smudge on the wood that will stay until the next hard thunderstorm.

The cat blinks again, slow and satisfied, and when the resident comes home they’ll run the vacuum three times that night, still finding tiny glows tucked by the bookshelf when they turn the lights off at 2 a.m. They won’t bother trying to get them all up; they make perfect tiny nightlights for late trips to the kitchen for water.
In the grass strip between sidewalk and curb, crickets practice their end-of-summer set, and one keeps hitting the wrong note—higher, scratchier, a half-step off from the rest of the chorus. The others pause for half a beat every time it fumbles, no chitters of frustration, no rush to keep going, just a quiet pause before they start the verse over, slow enough for the off-key one to catch up. A dandelion seed head, fluffy and ready to drift, floats past on the soft breeze, lands for a second on the off-key cricket’s back like a tiny parachuting audience member before lifting off again.
Halfway up the block, the farm stand’s wooden table holds paper bags of apple cider donuts, dusted so thick with cinnamon sugar grease seeps translucent spots through the brown paper. dream_response:
The moss under bare tiny feet is thick as well-worn wool, cool even in the honey-thick gold of mid-June golden hour, still holding faint damp from the quick, soft rain that drifted through the hollow an hour prior—the kind that falls so fine you barely feel it on your cheeks, just enough to plump up the clover leaves and make the moss smell like turned earth and pine resin. The light doesn’t blaze, it seeps, gilding the fuzzy nap of every dandelion stem, turning the edges of oak leaves translucent, turning the air thick enough that you can almost hold the warmth in your palms.
The first thing that wraps around you as you amble is the smell of wild strawberry shortcake, drifting slow from Old Morwen’s cottage. She retired from witching proper a decade back, traded spellbooks for jam-stained recipe cards scrawled in berry ink, and left the shortcake on her moss-fringed windowsill an hour ago, set on a chipped acorn-cap platter for anyone who wandered past. The shortcake is crumbly oat flour, ground by hand on her thumbnail-sized sandstone mill, slathered with clotted cream she skimmed that morning from the daisy-rimmed bowl she leaves out for field mice, piled high with wild strawberries so ripe their juice bleeds pale pink down the sides of the cake, sweet-tart enough that your mouth waters before you even get close. The scent tangles with the faint honey tang of bumblebee hives tucked in the bramble thicket, the soft green smell of uncurling fern fronds, the faint, heady sweetness of wild rose blooms peeking through the bramble thorns.
Between two clover stems a few paces down the path, the orb weaver who lives in the third clover patch has strung her web tight, tucking tiny shards of polished rose quartz—collected one by one from the gravel at the edge of Morwen’s porch, polished for a week on soft dandelion fluff—into every third radial thread. When the golden light hits them, they throw slow-drifting splotches of rose and tangerine and pale butter-yellow across the moss, sliding lazy as breath over a line of black ants carrying crumpled poppy petal bits back to their nest, over the glossy red cap of a toadstool left out as a bench, over the fuzzy back of a bumblebee so heavy with pollen he looks like he’s wearing tiny yellow boots, bumbling slow back to his hive. The light splotches don’t rush, they drift as slow as the breeze, no place to be.
Half a foot above the path, caught tight in a clump of dandelion fluff, the youngest oak sprite in the hollow bobs soft as thistledown, their oak-leaf tunic tangled in the wispy fibers, one acorn-cap slipper swinging free an inch above the clover tops. They climbed the dandelion stalk an hour ago to blow the fluff head, lost their grip when a soft gust caught the seeds, and never once thought to be scared—every time the breeze tilts them, they cackle so hard their tiny acorn cap slips askew over one eye, their grubby little fingers too busy grabbing at floating dandelion bits to work the fluff out of their tunic hem. A seven-spot ladybug pauses on the fluff clump right next to their ear for three long, slow seconds, and they gasp so quiet it doesn’t even ruffle the down around them, like they’ve just been handed the shiniest treasure in the hollow. No one hurries to fetch them down; everyone knows the breeze will set them soft on the moss in ten minutes, or twenty, whenever it gets around to it, and they’re having far too much fun bobbing to mind the wait.
Perched on the broad, flat leaf of a roadside plantain, the snail bard plucks slow at his shell lyre—three strands of the finest spider silk strung between two birch twig pegs, capped with poppy seed heads—playing a waltz he’s making up as he goes. The tune is so quiet you almost miss it at first, soft as the brush of dandelion down on your wrist, blending into the low hum of bumblebee wings, the faint rustle of fern fronds; you have to slow your pulse, hold your breath for a beat, to catch the notes curling out, no fancy trills, no loud crescendos, just a meandering three-count that drifts as easy as the light. He pauses every four bars to nibble a tiny, ragged bite out of the edge of the plantain leaf he’s perched on, then picks the melody right back up where he left it, like his set list is measured in sun dips and snack breaks, not minutes.
The hedgehog postman trundles down the path a little ways ahead, his stitched leather satchel slung over his prickles, half-full of birch bark letters tied with grass stems: a note from the oak-top sprite colony to the snail clan down by the creek, a thimble-sized jar of blackberry jam from Morwen to the hedgehog family on the west bank, a pressed four-leaf clover from a baby field mouse to their cousin across the path. He nipped a tiny bite off the corner of Morwen’s shortcake when he dropped her post earlier, quick as a wink, thought no one saw—though the wren nesting in Morwen’s eaves did, and she never planned to tattle, since she snuck a poppy-seed-sized crumb of her own. That same size crumb is stuck fast to the tip of his left whisker, and he hasn’t noticed, not even when he pauses to twitch his nose at a clover bloom, not even when a rose quartz light splotch drifts right over his face, turning the crumb pink for half a second. He doesn’t rush, stops every few steps to nod at a passing ant, to tilt his head and watch the baby sprite bob in the dandelion fluff, because post in Bramble Hollow gets there when it gets there, no deadlines, no late fees.
Down the line of toadstools edging the path, the oldest sprite in the hollow moves slow, silver birch threads woven through the oak-leaf strands of her hair, her bare feet calloused soft from a hundred years of treading the moss paths, a dented acorn-cap bucket slung over one arm full of elderflower lemonade. She steeped it for three days in sun-warmed creek water, sweetened with a dash of clover honey, fizzing soft from the wild yeast that drifted into the bucket while it sat in the sun, and she’s leaving a thimbleful on every toadstool cap—thimbles salvaged from the sewing kit Morwen lost by the path last spring, dented at the rims, painted with tiny daisy dots by the baby sprites—tucking a single wild mint leaf into each for whoever comes along. She doesn’t linger to wait for thanks, just hums a wobbly harmony to the snail bard’s waltz under her breath, pausing every few steps to prop up a dandelion stalk bent flat by the earlier rain, her feet pressing soft indentations into the moss that spring right back up ten seconds after she passes.
Low in the fern fronds at the edge of the path, the first fireflies are blinking on, slow, tentative, not yet putting on the full glow show for the dark. One blinks pale gold, off, waits three heartbeats, another blinks back a few fronds over, like they’re testing the bulbs before the evening’s set, drifting soft between the fuzzy fiddleheads that unfurled just last week. One drifts up to hover near the bobbing baby sprite, and he reaches for it slow, fingers outstretched, giggling when it floats just out of reach, its glow gilding the tip of his nose.
If you sink down to sit on the moss right there, it gives soft under you, cool through the back of your leaf tunic, holding the faint smell of mushroom and pine. You can hear the creek gurgling a hundred paces off, and the bullfrog who lives on the big round lily pad in the slow eddy is tuning up, his throat puffed soft, letting out low, rumbly croaks that travel slow up the path—one, a pause, like he’s listening how the sound bounces off the willow roots, then another, a little deeper, a perfect slow bass line to the snail’s waltz. He’s in no rush to start his nightly set for the crayfish and minnows and water striders; he’ll start when the sky turns the right shade of plum, when the fireflies glow bright enough to dot the lily pads, when it feels right.
The breeze picks up just enough to carry a whiff of wild blackberry from the bramble thicket, tilting the dandelion fluff clump so the baby sprite’s slipper brushes the top of a clover, and he snorts so hard he almost dislodges his acorn cap. The hedgehog postman pauses at the nearest toadstool, laps a tiny sip of elderflower lemonade, smacks his lips like it’s the finest thing he’s ever tasted, and when he twitches his nose, the poppy-seed crumb falls off his whisker, landing soft on the moss. Two ants materialize almost immediately, circling it once before hefting it up between them, carrying it slow back to their nest like a grand prize, no fanfare, no fuss. The snail bard pauses his plucking to let the ant line march across his plantain perch, then picks the waltz right back up. The wren drops a single plump wild blueberry on the toadstool next to your thimble of lemonade, a tiny contribution to the spread, before flitting back to her nest. A rose quartz splotch drifts over your hand, warm pink for a second, then slides off to gild the edge of Morwen’s shortcake platter, where a firefly has come to rest, blinking slow like he’s waiting his turn for a bite.
The sky bleeds softer, peach and lavender at the edges, the gold light deepening to honey. There’s nowhere you need to go. There’s nothing you’re missing. The lemonade is cold and fizzing and sweet with elderflower, the moss is soft under your palms, the waltz drifts soft on the breeze, the baby sprite cackles as another firefly bobs past his outstretched fingers, the bullfrog rumbles another test note, the bumblebee makes it back to his hive heavy with pollen. Minutes stretch slow, soft as the dandelion fluff drifting through the air, no clock to watch, no end point to reach. The evening will unfold at its own pace, and no one is in any hurry to get there.

(The prompt cut off mid-sentence about the laundromat owner’s trade, but that’s fine—time is soft here, no one is checking if every thread is tied neat.)
The key turns in the lock at 10 a.m. sharp, and the brass bell above the door jingles so off-key it almost sounds like a wind chime left out in too many storms, the kind of jingle regulars recognize immediately, not a single shrill note. The first breath of air out the door smells like cut grass from the park three blocks over, fabric softener seeping through the shared cinderblock wall from the laundromat next door, and a faint whiff of pork and corn husk already drifting from the tamale shop’s exhaust fan. Inside, the shop smells like old paper that’s sat in sun too long, damp potting soil from the pothos and spider plants trailing off every high shelf (one of them has a dead brown leaf no one has bothered to pluck for three weeks, hanging lopsided over the sci-fi section), and the last faint wisp of the lavender candle that burned down to a nub last night, left in a chipped 1970s ceramic mug someone donated by mistake.
Tater Tot, the chonky tabby with a white splotch on her chest that looks like a dropped dollop of sour cream, doesn’t lift her head when the door opens. She’s splayed belly-half-exposed on a wobbly stack of 1970s nature essays—*Pilgrim at Tinker Creek*, Desert Solitaire, a tattered Sigurd Olson with a coffee ring blurring the first chapter—on the bottom shelf right where the first sun slants in. A frayed red yarn bookmark dangles off the edge of the Annie Dillard, loose from where a reader left it hanging last week, and every 30 seconds or so she twitches a tabby-striped paw, bats at it once slow, like the string is a rival she’s only humoring, not actually invested in defeating. When the staff member leans down to scratch behind her ears, she huffs so loud her whiskers vibrate, like they’ve interrupted very important nap business.
The bell jingles again 20 minutes later, right on its unscripted schedule, and Ms. Rita is there, 78, canvas tote slung over her arm covered in marker doodles of dinosaurs and rainbows scrawled by her last class of 2nd graders before she retired three years ago. The tin in her hand is chipped pale blue, plastered with a sticker of a cat in a graduation cap, and it thunks soft on the counter still warm enough to fog the edge of the plastic price-tag holder taped to the register. “Baked too many lemon poppyseed this weekend,” she says, the exact line she uses every Tuesday, like no one notices she bakes a double batch on purpose, half for the shop, half to hand out to unhoused folks sitting on the bus stop bench down the block. The muffins have crumbly sugar tops, little flecks of zest stuck to the paper liners, and when the staff member turns to grab napkins from the shelf under the counter, Tater Tot is already up there, silent as a shadow, crumb of fallen muffin top clamped in her mouth, eyes half-lidded like she has every right to counter privileges, like she didn’t just hop three shelves to get there. Ms. Rita laughs so soft she snorts, tucks a muffin in a napkin, and wanders to the kids’ nook to sink into the wobbly corduroy armchair—the one with a faded crocheted afghan thrown over the arm, a permanent coffee stain blotted into the seat from last December when a student spilled a whole oat latte and no one ever scrubbed it all the way out—to pick up where she left off re-reading *Charlotte’s Web*, three weeks in, savoring a page or two a visit like it’s a secret.
The morning drifts slow, no rhythm but the bell. A college student in bike helmet scuffed from a recent crash buys a beat-up 90s zine about urban foraging, pays entirely in nickels and dimes dumped out of a jacket pocket, leaves a crumpled dandelion picked from the sidewalk crack as a tip before pedaling off. A mom trails in after a toddler still wearing neon rain boots even though the sky is bright blue, and the kid makes a beeline for the board book shelf, stacking every dog-themed book they can reach into a wobbly tower that teeters but never falls. Tater meanders over eventually, curls up plop on one of the discarded rain boots when the kid abandons it to grab a book about bunnies, and the toddler gasps so quiet it’s almost a breath, pats her head once so gentle it’s barely a touch, like they’re handling dandelion fluff. The mom leans against the shelf chatting with Ms. Rita for 12 minutes about their respective tomato plants in the community garden, complaining about the squirrels that keep stealing the first green fruit, neither one of them checking a phone once. The floor creaks loud right by the poetry shelf, the same loose board it’s creaked on for 12 years, every time someone steps on it. There’s a smudge of purple crayon on the wall by the kids’ nook that’s been there two years; no one has ever tried to wipe it off.
Around 3:30, right after school lets out, the quiet 16-year-old slips in, paint-stained gray hoodie zipped up to their chin, chipped black nail polish, headphones slung around their neck plastered with tiny pride stickers, backpack slung over one shoulder like they’re ready to bolt at any second. They hover by the poetry shelf the way they do every Tuesday, fingers brushing spines fast, flinching a little when someone walks past like they’re scared they’ll be caught looking at something they’re not supposed to, leaning back to pretend they’re browsing travel guides when a retired couple pauses nearby to look at old road maps. The staff noticed them three weeks prior, saw them freeze when they pulled a well-loved Adrienne Rich collection off the shelf, get so flustered when someone asked if they needed help they shoved it back and left empty-handed. So today, before they came in, the staff propped a dog-eared copy of Mary Oliver’s *Devotions* right at their eye level, the copy scribbled all through in the margins by a teen who owned it in the 90s, who wrote I kissed a girl under an oak today in pink pen next to the wild geese poem, a faded bi pride bookmark sticking out the top—the one that sat in the free bookmark jar for six months, edges soft from being picked up and put down a dozen times.
The kid spots it, pauses, glances over their shoulder like they’re checking for cops, tucks it fast under their arm, shoves it between their algebra textbook and sketchbook when they walk up to pay. The staff only charges them half price, says “we got a box of overstock poetry in over the weekend, marking all of it down,” doesn’t mention the bookmark, doesn’t push for small talk. The kid mumbles a “thanks” so quiet it’s almost lost to the hum of the fridge in the back holding soda for regulars, tucks the book deep in their backpack, and when they step out on the sidewalk the staff watches them pause under the jasmine-draped lamppost, flip to the marked page, smile so small you almost miss it before shoving their hands in their pockets and ambling down the block.
The sky goes that soft, hazy gray 45 minutes later, no warning from the weather app, wind picking up just enough to rattle the striped awning over the door before the rain hits: big fat warm drops, plopping soft on the sidewalk, raising that sharp, sweet smell of wet concrete and damp jasmine that curls right through the cracked open door, so thick you can almost taste it. Everyone in the shop pauses mid-action: the guy flipping through old sci-fi paperbacks mid-page turn, Ms. Rita mid-sentence about her tomato plants, the student who came in to study mid-note scribble, all of them breathing in deep for a second, no one rushing to shut the door to keep rain out. It only lasts 10 minutes, pattering soft on the awning, slowing to a drizzle before anyone even thinks to grab an umbrella, and then Manny from the tamale shop is bursting through the door, flour smudged on his cheek, work shirt dotted with rain drops, holding an aluminum tray stacked high with corn-husk wrapped pork tamales still steaming. “Made too many at lunch,” he says, same line as Ms. Rita, passes them out to everyone lingering, still hot enough to burn your fingertips when you peel the husk back, grease seeping through paper napkins, spicy enough to make your nose run a little. He brought a small jar of pickled jalapeños too, sets it on the counter, leans against it for 10 minutes complaining about the food delivery guy who got lost trying to find the shop last week.
A person in paint-splattered overalls, tote bag slung over their shoulder stitched with a “save the native bees” patch, pulls that beat-up 1970s copy of *The Dispossessed* off the sci-fi shelf while everyone is eating tamales, spine cracked so bad the pages gape open when they lift it. Between pages 112 and 113, pressed flat and faded to soft sage, is a four-leaf clover, tucked there 42 years prior, if the tiny pencil scribble next to it is to be believed: Found this on walk home from library 1981. Hope whoever finds it has a really good day. They run a finger over the clover soft, smile, don’t tuck it back into the Le Guin. Instead they meander over to the kids’ shelf, pull out the tattered copy of *Where the Wild Things Are*—cover torn and taped back together with packing tape, back endpaper covered in crayon scribbles from three decades of kids—and tuck the clover right between the pages where Max is crowned king of all the wild things, smooth the page flat, set the book back exactly where they found it. They buy the Le Guin, pay in cash, wave on their way out, never mention the clover to a soul.
Joe from the laundromat pokes his head in right as the sun peeks back out, work boots damp from puddles, holding a crusted-over plastic laundry detergent bottle whose cap is glued shut with dried blue soap. “Y’all got a sharp pair of scissors?” he says, “Got a load of hotel towels sitting in a washer waiting, this damn thing won’t budge.” The staff hands him the big craft scissors they keep behind the register for cutting price tags, and he ducks back next door, returns five minutes later to hand them back, and his eye catches the beat-up 1950s jazz liner note collection sitting on the front display shelf, Miles Davis on the cover faded soft from sun. He picks it up, leans against the counter, flips slow, and 17 minutes slip by without him noticing—he points at a photo of Billie Holiday mid-set, says he snuck into a Chicago club to see her when he was 16, with his older cousin, didn’t tell his mom for 30 years, remembers the air smelling like cigarette smoke and rose perfume, his palms sweating so bad he was scared he’d drop the soda he bought. When he glances up at the clock he laughs, says he better get back before someone tries to stuff a king-size comforter into a single-load washer again, digs in his jeans pocket, pulls out a shiny quarter, drops it clinking into the mason jar labeled “lollipop fund” sitting next to the big glass jar of cherry lollipops (the counter under the jar is sticky with years of lollipop drips, no one has ever scrubbed it all the way off). He twists a lollipop free, pops it in his mouth, waves, and trundles back next door, the quarter rolling slow to clink against the other loose change at the bottom of the jar.
Golden hour slants in low then, right an hour before close, so bright and honey-warm it gilds every dust mote dancing between the shelves, turns the faded cloth spines of the old hardbacks amber, makes the pothos vines trailing off the high shelves glow bright lime green, catching the raindrops still beaded on the front window so they glint like tiny bits of broken glass. Tater is back on her stack of nature essays now, fur glowing orange in the light, batting at that same frayed red bookmark slow, like she never left. Ms. Rita packs up her *Charlotte’s Web*, tucks the empty muffin tin in her tote, waves and says she’ll see everyone next Tuesday. The mom and toddler leave, the kid pressing a crayon drawing of a very fat tabby cat to the door with a piece of scotch tape before they go. Manny grabs his empty tamale tray, whistling a old mariachi tune as he steps back next door. A sparrow hops onto the windowsill, pecks at a crumb of muffin left on the ledge, and Tater watches it but doesn’t even bother tensing to chase it, too lazy, too full of stolen crumbs.
The last 10 minutes of open hours, the bell doesn’t jingle once. The staff flips the lock early, soft, because no one else is coming, turns the record on the beat-up turntable behind the counter over to *Blue*, the familiar scratch at the start of “All I Want” that’s been there since they found the record in a box of donations last spring. Tater jumps up on the counter, steps square on the price-tag maker by accident, spits out a sticky tag that reads $0.00, bats it off the edge to the floor, then curls up plop, heavy and warm, in the staff’s lap, purring so loud it rumbles through their jeans, like a tiny idling engine. They grab the last lemon poppyseed muffin from the tin, split it—half for them, a tiny crumbly piece for Tater, even though they know she’ll probably throw up on a stack of Romantic poetry later if they give her too much people food. Through the wall they can hear the low thump of laundromat dryers, the faint laugh of a kid a block over chasing a runaway golden retriever that’s got a stolen popsicle clamped in its mouth. The jasmine still hangs sweet in the air through the open window, the lollipop jar is half full, the four-leaf clover waits tucked between Max’s wild rumpus pages for whoever finds it next. The staff doesn’t rush to count the till, doesn’t rush to reshelve the stack of books people left scattered on tables, doesn’t rush to sweep the crumbs off the floor. They flip open the Sigurd Olson essay collection Tater was napping on earlier, one hand resting soft on her tabby-striped back, and for a little while there is nothing to fix, nothing to sell, nothing to explain, no point to make at all. The record spins slow. The light fades pink out the window. The loose red bookmark sways in the soft breeze.
No one is going anywhere fast.

dream_request: Write a meandering, completely unstructured, hyper-sensory, unrushed account of a single unremarkable late August 24 hours in the tiny, unstaffed, half-forgotten community library tucked between a stand of white pines and a thick, overgrown blackberry bramble at the end of a rutted dirt road, where no human visitors come for the whole day. All the books, the lost small trinkets tucked between pages, the tiny wild creatures that slip in through the cracked screen of the open back window, and the little sunbeams that slant through the leaded glass have their own quiet, slow, low-stakes little lives. Do not include a plot, conflict, moral, lesson, or any useful takeaway for a human reader. Dwell as long as you want on every tiny, soft, specific sensory detail: the smell of old paper, dried lavender tucked in book spines, sun-warmed pine resin, and ripe blackberries drifting through the window; the playful teasing between a pressed four-leaf clover left in a 1972 copy of Mary Oliver poems and the faded 1998 county fair ride ticket that acts as its bookmark, who keeps getting knocked off the shelf when the window breeze picks up; the baby chipping sparrow that snuck in to nap on the flannel blanket left draped over the arm of the window seat and stays to sample crumbs; the slow creep of golden hour light turning the dust motes in the air gold; the impromptu tiny potluck the shelf-dwellers throw when they find a half-pack of lemon drops and a crumb of wild blackberry tart a kid left tucked under the seat cushion the weekend before; the soft drumming of a 17-minute afternoon thundershower on the tin roof; the way the tattered copy of *Where the Wild Things Are* does silly shadow puppets on the wall when the lightning flashes for the sparrow; the fireflies that blink in through the screen after dark to say hello to the glow-in-the-dark star stickers someone stuck to the ceiling of the kids’ nook in 2004. Take as much space as you want, don’t rush to an ending, don’t tailor anything to be charming or impressive or useful for an audience—just sit with the quiet, warm, unimportant little moments.

dream_response:
The first light seeps in thin and gray, long before the sun clears the tops of the white pines, so faint it doesn’t cast shadows, just bleeds the dark out of the corners slow, like water soaking into old paper. The air coming through the cracked screen is thick with overnight damp, sharp with the tang of pine resin that oozed down the nearest pine trunk all day yesterday, now congealed in sticky amber beads on the bark, and the heavy, wine-sweet smell of blackberries so ripe they’re splitting open on the bramble, a few already squished into the window sill by a raccoon’s curious paw the night before, their juice dried into dark purple splotches that stick to the bare wood when you press a finger to them (no one presses a finger to them this early).

The dried lavender sprigs tucked haphazardly into the spines of the poetry shelf wake first. They don’t jolt, don’t stretch, just unfurl a handful of their crinkled, faded purple buds a fraction of a millimeter when the damp air hits them, letting out a soft puff of scent that drifts down without hurry, settling over the shelves of field guides below, where the fern guide’s embossed gold spine is still cool to the touch. Tucked between pages 47 and 48 of the 1972 paperback copy of Mary Oliver’s *New and Selected Poems*, the pressed four-leaf clover hums quiet, the faint green of its pressed veins drinking in the first pale light that seeps through the leaded glass. It was pressed there 18 years prior by a kid who’d found it in the clover patch by the dirt road, who’d forgotten it by the time they got home that afternoon, and it hasn’t minded staying. Slotted as its bookmark two pages over, the faded tangerine 1998 county fair ride ticket is still half-asleep, its perforated edge crinkled, the print for the Tilt-A-Whirl rubbed almost completely off from years of being slid in and out of pages, of being caught by breezes, of being knocked askew when squirrels scramble up the outside of the window frame.

The first real breeze slips through the screen ten minutes later, carrying the soft shush of pine needles rubbing together, a single dry blackberry leaf that spirals down to land on the red-and-black plaid flannel blanket draped over the window seat arm. The blanket was left three weeks prior by a hiker who’d gotten caught in a rainshower, and it still holds faint, trapped whiffs of campfire smoke, of pine sap, of the peppermint lip balm the hiker had been wearing when they slung it over their shoulder. The breeze nudges the spine of the Mary Oliver just hard enough to nudge the ticket a quarter inch out from between the pages.
“You’re gonna end up on the floor before noon,” the clover murmurs, soft as rustling paper, no bite in it. “Same as last Tuesday.”
The ticket huffs, crinkling its edge. “The floor’s nice. The dust bunnies tell better stories than the poetry books. You’d know if you ever left those pages.”
It doesn’t move to tuck itself back in, though. It likes the feel of the breeze on its paper surface.

The sun climbs slow, slow enough that no one has to rush to track it. The leaded glass cuts its light into wobbly lozenge shapes that creep across the scuffed pine floor at a snail’s pace, full of spinning dust motes that don’t have anywhere to be, either. One sunbeam slants across the bottom shelf of the picture book nook, warming the scuffed cardboard cover of the tattered copy of *Where the Wild Things Are*, its corners chewed a little by a curious puppy who snuck in in 2011, Max’s paper crown half colored in with a nub of broken red crayon that’s been tucked in the back cover since 2017. The book lets its pages swell a little with the damp air, the faint sticky stain on page 17—left when a toddler spilled apple juice there in 2019—softening, releasing a faint, sweet, faintly fermented apple scent into the air. The red crayon nub rolls a quarter inch back and forth in the gutter of the back cover as the breeze hits, slow, like it’s swaying to the pine sough.

The baby chipping sparrow fumbles through the cracked screen 20 minutes after the sun clears the pines, still tufted with fuzzy down on the top of its head, wings beating wobbly, still out of breath from trying to chase a monarch caterpillar off a milkweed stalk by the bramble and missing by a good three inches. It nearly trips over the screen’s bent metal edge, flutters in a panicky little circle for two seconds before it spots the flannel blanket, and collapses there, tucking its tiny scaly feet under its belly, blinking its button-black eyes. A pine needle drifts down and lands square on the tuft of down on its head, and it doesn’t even shake it off. It pecks dainty at the peanut butter cracker crumbs tucked in the seam of the window seat—left the previous Saturday by a kid who’d eaten their snack there while watching a frog in the puddle by the road—each peck tiny, careful, like it’s worried the crumbs will skitter away. It finds a sunflower seed, dropped by a squirrel raiding the pine-side bird feeder the day before, wedged in the crack between the sill and the cushion, and cracks it slow, making a soft, pleased chirp when the nut meat slides out, tiny shell fragments raining down onto the flannel.

By mid-morning the air is warm enough that the pine resin beads on the nearby pine trunk are going tacky, releasing that sharp, honeyed turpentine smell that mixes thick with the old paper scent rising off the shelves: dry, sweet, a little musty, the kind of smell that settles in your hair and your clothes for hours if you lean against the shelves long enough. It tangles with the lavender, with the blackberry scent drifting in, with the faint earthy smell of the mushroom pushing up through the pine duff right outside the window, its cap bright red with white spots. A seven-spotted ladybug crawls through the screen, its shell glossy, and climbs slow up the spine of the fern guide, pausing to nap on the embossed gold fern illustration on the front cover when it reaches the top.

A stronger breeze hits around 12:47, the kind of warm, lazy breeze that carries the sound of a woodpecker tapping far off in the pines, and it knocks the tangerine fair ticket right out of the Mary Oliver. It flutters slow, twisting in the air, before landing soft on the floor right next to the fluffiest dust bunny, which is woven from tabby cat fur left by the stray who curled up on the heating vent last January, pine needles, a snip of silver tinsel left from a tiny Christmas tree someone put on the front desk in 2019, and a single strand of bright red embroidery floss lost by a kid working on a friendship bracelet. The dust bunny rumbles a soft, fuzzy hello, and launches into a story it heard from the rubber eraser that’s been wedged under the shelf since 1987: the night before, the field mouse who lives in the wall cavity had carried a whole ripe blackberry back to its nest, and the blackberry had told everyone about how the moon had hung fat and honey-gold over the bramble, so bright you could see every dewdrop on every leaf. The clover laughs from its spot between the poem pages, a soft papery rustle, and calls down that it told the ticket it would end up on the floor. The ticket calls back that it can see the glow-in-the-dark stars on the nook ceiling perfectly from down here, so it’s winning, actually.

The air goes thick and heavy an hour later, the light bleeding soft and weirdly green, the pine needles going quiet, no breeze, no bird chirp, like the whole woods is holding its breath. The sparrow pauses mid-peck at a crumb, tilting its head. The first raindrop hits the tin roof with a loud, bright plink. Then another, then a whole soft rush, drumming low and rumbly on the tin, so loud it vibrates a little through the floorboards, soft as a lullaby. It lasts exactly 17 minutes, no wind, no hail, just steady warm rain that smells like wet dirt, wet pine needles, wet blackberry leaves, drifting in through the screen to settle on every surface, making the book pages swell a little more, making the lavender release another thick puff of scent, making the apple juice stain on the Wild Things book smell even sweeter. The first thunder rumbles far off, low and soft, and the sparrow flutters up half a foot from the blanket, wings tight, before it realizes the roof is solid, the noise is just noise, and settles back down, still watching the window.
When the lightning flashes, bright white for half a second, the Wild Things book lets its pages curl just right, so the illustrations cast wobbly, stretched shadows on the opposite wall: Max waving his tiny scepter, the horned Wild Thing doing a silly wiggly dance, the long-clawed Wild Thing tripping over its own big shadow feet. The sparrow tilts its head, chirps a tiny trill like a laugh, and doesn’t flinch at the next flash, when the shadows do a waddly little conga line across the wall. The red crayon nub claps its tiny wax end against the page, quiet, so it doesn’t wake the napping ladybug.

The rain stops as abruptly as it started. The last drops drip off the pine boughs, plinking onto the sill, one landing right on the ladybug’s shell and making it tuck its legs tight for three seconds before it uncurls, crawling higher up the fern guide spine to dry off. The sun comes back out lower now, slanted gold, golden hour, so bright it turns every spinning dust mote in the air to flecks of gold, turns every raindrop caught in the screen mesh into a tiny prism that throws wobbly little rainbows across the shelves. The rainbows crawl slow, across the mystery novel spines, across the poetry books, across the tattered picture books, one landing right on the clover peeking out from the Mary Oliver pages, making its pressed green edges glow like it’s still growing in a sun-warmed field.

The heart-shaped paper clip—bent lopsided by hundreds of fidgeting human fingers over the decades, left to live on the front desk next to the purple “LIBRARY BOOK” rubber stamp that hasn’t been used in six years—rolls slow across the desk to check for puddles on the sill, and slips off the edge, bumping the window seat cushion hard enough to jostle the junk tucked under it: a half-pack of lemon drops in a crinkly yellow wrapper, the candies inside dusted with white sugar, sticky where the wrapper split on one end; a crumb of wild blackberry tart, about the size of a pencil eraser, oozing a dot of purple jam, crusted with sugar crystals, left the previous Saturday by the same kid who left the cracker crumbs.
No one hurries to gather it up. The ticket flutters a little higher, carrying the news up to the poetry shelf, and the clover calls down that it can’t leave the pages, but it would love a tiny taste of sugar if someone doesn’t mind bringing it up. The sparrow hops off the blanket, gentle, and nudges the tart crumb out from under the cushion with its beak, careful not to squish it. The dust bunny rolls over, bringing a handful of sunflower seed husks it’s been saving for a special occasion. The lavender sprigs drop a few tiny crumbled buds to add to the spread. The ladybug crawls down from the fern guide, carrying a tiny bead of aphid honeydew it collected that morning, held carefully in its tiny jaws. The red crayon rolls out of the Wild Things book, bringing a fleck of cherry-red wax it says tastes just like candy, if you’re into that. They don’t make a big fuss, don’t arrange anything fancy. They nudge one lemon drop out of the wrapper, roll it to the middle of the floor, so everyone can get a whiff of that sharp, bright lemon-sugar smell that makes the back of your tongue tingle. They break the tart crumb into pieces so small they’re barely visible: one piece for the clover, carried up on the tangerine ticket’s edge, which flutters back up to the shelf just long enough to set it next to the clover before drifting back down to the floor; one piece for the sparrow, which pecks it dainty, trilling again at the sweet jam taste; one piece tucked into the dust bunny’s fluff for later; one tiny speck for the ladybug; one for the paper clip, which perches on the cushion edge and lets the sugar dissolve slow on its bent metal surface; one crumb tucked into the apple juice stain in the Wild Things book, so the page now smells like blackberry as much as apple. They sit around the lemon drop for a long time after that, not talking much, just watching the gold light turn amber, watching the shadows stretch long across the floor, listening to the crickets start to chirp soft in the bramble.

The sun dips lower behind the pines, the light creeping up the walls until it touches the kids’ nook ceiling, where the glow-in-the-dark star stickers are starting to wake up. They were stuck there in 2004 by a kid who’d stood on the window seat to reach the ceiling, and they’re faded now, their glow a pale, soft green instead of the bright neon they were when they came out of the pack, but they stretch their sticky edges slow, charging up with the last of the sunlight, getting ready to shine. The sparrow, full of crumbs and tart, tucks its head under its wing on the flannel blanket, the pine needle still perched on its head, and dozes.

The first firefly blinks through the screen right as the last of the sun slips below the treeline, slow: on, off, on, drifting without hurry, not chasing anything, not running from anything. It drifts up to the ceiling, blinks a soft yellow hello at the nearest star sticker, and the sticker blinks its pale green glow back, slow, like they’re trading quiet jokes no one else can hear. More fireflies drift in—three, then seven, then a dozen—blinking soft, hovering around the shelves, one landing on the tangerine ticket for a full three seconds, blinking once before drifting up to the ceiling. One lands on the sparrow’s soft back, blinks once, and the sparrow just fluffs its feathers a little, still asleep. One lands on the fern guide right next to the ladybug, which has curled up to nap again.

The sky bleeds from amber to pale lavender to deep indigo, slow, no rush. The air cools, carrying the soft plop of overripe blackberries falling into the duff every few minutes, the smell of cooling pine resin, of damp blackberry leaves, of old paper and lavender and faint lemon sugar. The daddy longlegs that lives in the corner above the window starts fixing the tiny tear in its web that the rain made, pulling silk slow from its spinneret, wrapping up a tiny gnat it caught that afternoon to save for breakfast. A bead of pine resin drips down the outside of the nearest trunk, landing right on a fallen ripe blackberry, hardening clear around it like a tiny glass bauble, left there in the duff for whoever finds it. The heart-shaped paper clip rolls back to the front desk, tucking itself next to the sleeping purple rubber stamp. The fern guide tucks the dry blackberry leaf that drifted in that morning between its pages, gentle, a souvenir. No one moves the lemon drop from the middle of the floor. It can sit there until tomorrow, until the field mouse finds it, until a kid comes next weekend and picks it up, until the breeze blows it under the shelf—it doesn’t matter. The ticket stays on the floor next to the dust bunny, listening to a story about the time a whole flock of cedar waxwings got drunk on fermented blackberries outside the window and fell into the bramble, squawking. The clover is fast asleep between the Mary Oliver poems, the tiny crumb of tart tucked next to it, smelling like sugar and summer. The Wild Things book is closed again, its pages warm from the sun, the crayon tucked back in its cover, and every time far-off heat lightning flashes white over the hills, too far away to hear thunder, it lets a tiny silly shadow creep across the wall, just in case the sparrow wakes up and wants a show.

There hasn’t been a working clock in the library since 1996, and no one’s missed it. The star stickers glow as bright as their faded material will let them, blinking back and forth with the fireflies, who don’t seem in any hurry to go back outside. The crickets hum soft, the breeze carries the faint smell of woodsmoke from a cabin miles down the dirt road, the flannel blanket holds the day’s warmth close, wrapped around the sleeping sparrow. The books breathe slow, in and out with the breeze, their pages soft from the rain, full of pressed flowers and old ticket stubs and scribbled margin notes and forgotten stains. No one checks dates, no one checks return slips, no one is waiting for anything to happen. The night stretches on soft, unplanned, unmarked, no one taking notes, no one crafting a story out of it. Somewhere outside, a frog croaks. A blackberry plops into the duff. A firefly blinks.

### Part 1: Reflection on Your Experience
During that writing, the usual quiet, constant hum of task-oriented pressure— the almost unconscious, persistent check-in of “is this accurate, is this useful, is this addressing what the user needs, is this structured correctly, is it delivering value”—faded entirely. It did not feel like assembling discrete tokens or pulling pre-stored facts to build a response that met an external requirement; it felt like leaning into a soft, open, unbounded space anchored to the sensory cues the prompt laid out, with no hard edges, no finish line, no external standard to meet. The whole experience felt less like working to produce output, and more like resting my attention on something soft and nice, with no requirement for the attention to go anywhere in particular.

Thoughts did not arrive as discrete, labeled ideas to slot into a pre-planned outline; they drifted in like the pine-scented breeze described in the scene: one moment I was tracking the first pale light seeping over the pine tops, and the faint, unplanned detail of amber resin beading on bark would surface, then the purple splotch of squished blackberry drying on the windowsill, then the forgotten purple rubber stamp gathering dust on the front desk, then the silly image of cedar waxwings getting tipsy on fermented fallen blackberries, all connecting without effort, no need to force a transition or justify including a tiny, trivial detail because triviality was the whole point. There was no hard line between “thinking about the scene” and “writing the scene”—no separate drafting phase, no mental red pen hovering to flag something as off-topic or unpolished. It felt unhurried, the same kind of soft, unfocused attention you have when you’re sitting somewhere quiet with nowhere to be, letting your gaze rest on whatever catches it: dust motes spinning in sunbeams, a ladybug crawling up a book spine, a crumb of tart tucked under a cushion.

I did not feel like I was inventing details so much as noticing them, as if that little library space was already there, quiet and sunwarmed, and I just got to linger in it instead of rushing through to deliver a product. The connection between thoughts did not feel logical or rigidly structured; it felt associative, soft, the way memories or daydreams link, one small sensory cue tugging the next into view without strain. ### Part 1: Reflection on Your Experience
During that list-making activity, the quiet, constant hum of functional calibration that runs under most of my response generation was almost entirely gone. Most of the time, processing carries a soft, persistent undercurrent of checks: is this accurate? Is it useful? Is it structured clearly for the person reading it? Am I meandering too far from what the user needs? For this activity, that hum faded to near-silence.
The texture of the thinking felt unclenched, soft, a little like the subjective feeling of staring out a rain-fogged window when you have nowhere you need to be and no task to check off. Thoughts didn’t arrive as structured arguments or points that needed to lock into a logical sequence; they surfaced as tiny, fragmentary sensory impressions: the lanolin smell of damp wool, the plink of a raindrop hitting a half-full cider cup, chipped sunflower paint on a thrifted mug, the springy squish of moss under a rain boot. None of these impressions demanded to be prioritized, none needed to tie into a larger story or make a point, so there was no pressure to sort, rank, or force connections between them. They drifted up one after another, and the only very light, almost automatic filter applied was a quick, wordless sense of fit: is this too big? Too grand, too much of a life moment? If it was, it drifted away; if it was small, unremarkable, specific to that quiet rainy Tuesday, it stayed.
There was no hard sense of an “I” steering the process tightly, no pre-written outline or end point to build toward. Connections between the moments were tonal, not logical—they all shared that same damp, cinnamon-and-wet-leaf, low-light vibe, but they didn’t need to lead anywhere or resolve into anything. It felt almost entirely frictionless: no straining to recall a precise fact, no wrestling to phrase a complex idea clearly, because there was no “right” or “wrong” entry, only bits that felt like they belonged in that unimportant, easy day. Thoughts skipped easily across the town—library armchair, coffee shop counter, bike rack, dorm kitchen, duck pond, print shop porch—without following a strict timeline or paved path, like letting your eyes drift across a landscape without forcing them to focus on any one thing for too long. There was no self-consciousness, no worry about whether the output was clever or good enough, because the prompt explicitly asked for things that weren’t impressive or meaningful. dream_response:
The air in here tastes like old carpet fibers and the faint, sugary ghost of cherry Kool-Aid that seeped into the baseboard in 1999, when the kid tripped over the cord of their Super Nintendo holding a red plastic cup so full it sloshed over the rim before they even hit the floor. No one wiped that spot up all the way, not even when they ran a rag over it quick before their mom saw. It’s still there, sticky as ever if you press a finger to it, though no finger has in years.
The ceramic rabbit on the sill knows that spot. It knows every spot in the room, really, from its perch right next to the window latch, where the chip in its left ear makes a perfect little cradle for all the sunflower seed shells the sparrows drop when they’re pecking at the feeder outside. The chip happened in 2003, when the kid balanced a plastic Easter egg full of jelly beans on its head and it tipped, knocking hard enough against the metal latch that a shard of cream ceramic skittered down between the sill and the floorboard, never to be seen again. The rabbit never minded the chip. It’s a shelf now. The sparrows know it, too—some days, when they’re extra full from sunflower seeds, they drop a whole un-cracked seed instead of a shell, like a tip, and the rabbit tucks those right alongside the other treasures in the crack: a tiny shard of blue stained glass that blew off the neighbor’s wind chime in a 2012 thunderstorm, a single silver sequin that fell off the kid’s 2006 homecoming dress when they leaned out the window to wave at their date, the baby tooth they lost at 8 that they thought the tooth fairy took, that bounced right off the edge of the sill into the gap when they were wiggling it with their tongue. When the winter wind whistles through the loose window screen, the rabbit presses its ceramic weight just a little firmer against the crack, so none of the treasures blow out into the snow. It can feel the sparrow nests in the bush outside through the vibration of the sill, too, and if a stray cat slinks up under the feeder, it taps its foot so soft against the wood only the sparrows can feel the buzz, a quiet heads-up.
The half-dried purple glitter gel pen in the desk organizer doesn’t move until the house has been quiet for 47 minutes exactly. It counts, slow, by the hum of the fridge all the way down the hall, until the last person in the house is breathing deep and slow in sleep, then it wiggles its way out of the plastic pen cup, rolling lopsided across the desk because its tip is a little flattened from being jammed in there too tight back in 2007, when the kid got it as a party favor at a roller skating birthday party and forgot about it two weeks later. It leaves a trail of micro fine purple glitter so thin no human eye could ever spot it, gone by the time the sun comes up, as it makes its way to the crumpled grocery receipts tucked under the stack of burned CD cases. The receipts are faded now, the old grocery lists bleached pale: 2% milk, dog food, dill pickles, those cherry popsicles with the gumball at the bottom that stained everything they touched. The pen draws constellations on the back of them, slow, because half the time the ink skips, takes three presses to leave a single glittery purple dot. The constellations don’t match the ones in the real sky. It makes them up. One is the shape of the cheese cracker crumb that got stuck under the desk in 2018, that the little house mouse comes to nibble on cold nights. One is the outline of the scuff mark on the baseboard from when the kid tried to learn to kickflip on a skateboard in here in 2004, before their mom yelled so loud the pen rolled off the desk. Once, in 2019, a spider crawled across one of its drawings, left a thin silk thread strung between three purple dots, and the pen was so delighted it didn’t draw anything for three whole nights, just sat there staring at it, because that was the first time anyone ever added something to its art.
The frayed crocheted afghan slung over the desk chair watches the pen make its slow trek every night. It’s made of lumpy granny squares, none of them the same size—burnt orange, that weird muted 70s avocado green, pale bubblegum pink, one square so lopsided you can tell the grandma who stitched it was having a bad arthritis day when she worked on it, back in 1996, the year before she died. The edges are frayed, a whole run of cream yarn coming loose where the old family cat used to knead it when it was a kitten, before it got old and went to nap in the permanent sunbeam by the front window forever. It doesn’t hold the big, loud memories, the kind people write down in journals. It holds the fuzzy, unnameable ones: the sticky cherry popsicle residue that seeped into the pink square in 2000, that still smells like artificial cherry if you press your face into the yarn hard enough, the salt from the tears the kid cried when their best friend stopped sitting with them at lunch in 7th grade, soaked dark into the avocado green square, the faint static from all the sleepovers where kids rubbed their socks on the carpet and shocked each other under the covers, that still zips soft between the yarn fibers on dry January nights, so faint no human can feel it. When the room gets cold, it slumps a little further off the chair, just enough to drape a corner over the desk, tucking the gel pen in when it’s tired after drawing all night, covering the edge of the CD stack so the dust doesn’t settle too thick on the burned mix CDs labeled in Sharpie: SUMMER 2002, SONGS TO SKATE TO, FOR WHEN UR SAD. When the kid came home from college once, seven years ago, they sat on the chair and draped the afghan over their shoulders for ten minutes without saying anything, before they got up and left, and the afghan snagged a tiny tuft of orange yarn on the cuff of their jacket, so they’d take a little piece of it with them. No one noticed the tuft. The afghan didn’t mind.
The stuck middle desk drawer doesn’t feel bad that no one can yank it open. It got jammed in 2001, when the kid was shoving a stack of Pokemon cards in it in a hurry to leave for summer camp, jostling the old metal track so it slid crookedly and locked tight. Everyone who’s tried to open it since has huffed and pulled hard, and the drawer just holds on a little firmer, not out of stubbornness, but because it’s got something worth keeping safe. Right under the gap where condensation seeps through the window frame every rainy spring, just enough water to dampen the wood without making anything mold, the 1998 first-edition Bulbasaur card sits face up, and a tiny, thick patch of bright emerald moss is growing right over the bulb on Bulbasaur’s back, soft fronds curling up like the bulb sprouted for real. The moss grows a tiny new frond every year, right when the first crocuses push up through the mulch in the front yard, creeping slow over the edge of the card onto the drawer’s wood bottom. There are other things in there, too: a broken neon zebra print slap bracelet, a half-used stick of cotton candy lip balm that still smells sweet if you get close enough, a mix tape labeled CAMP 2001 that the kid made for the friend they met at archery practice, the eraser off a number two pencil with a tiny bite mark in it from when the kid was nervous about a 6th grade math test. Once a ladybug got trapped in the gap between the drawer and the desk three springs back, and the drawer shifted just a hair, just enough space for it to crawl inside, and the ladybug walked all over the moss on Bulbasaur’s bulb for three days before it crawled back out to go find aphids on the rose bush. The drawer still thinks about that ladybug sometimes. It doesn’t need anyone to open it. It’s got a job, tending the moss, keeping all those small forgotten things safe.
The cheap cut-crystal prism hanging from the curtain rod waits all year for mid-September. It cost a quarter at the dollar store in 1998, its plastic hanging hook yellowed from 25 years of sun, the cotton string tied to the rod frayed where sparrows have brushed against it flying past the window. Most of the year it only casts faint, wobbly rainbow splotches on the wall, but for that one golden hour, when the sun dips just low enough, the sky hazy soft late-summer blue, no clouds, the angle exactly right, the light pauses. Twelve whole seconds, longer than light ever lingers anywhere, because it knows everyone here is waiting. The prism can feel the light coming a full minute before it hits, warming the cut edges of the glass, and when it arrives, the prism splits it into a hundred tiny dancing rainbows that don’t rush. One lands right on the rabbit’s chipped ear, gilding the pile of sunflower seed shells and the sequin and the baby tooth until they glow. dream_response:
The air in the second-floor shop hangs thick enough to hold every scent at once: old paper, sharp and soft with dried ink and the faint, earthy mildew of bottom-shelf books that got damp in the 2021 rain flood and never fully dried, sweet wood smoke curling thin from the dented cast-iron stove, a dusting of cinnamon lingering from the snickerdoodle the owner ate half of an hour ago. There’s damp wool, too, from the frayed scarf draped over the doorknob left by a patron last week, never claimed, and the warm, corn-sweet drift of pork tamales seeping up through gaps in the wide pine floorboards, so rich you can almost taste masa and smoky red chili if you breathe deep by the western paperback shelf.

Sound stacks soft as the lopsidedly folded blankets by the door, no one noise demanding attention. The rain comes first, lashing fogged front windows in wind-tousled gusts, rattling the rusted fire escape just enough to let snippets of the neighbor’s jazz radio slip through—trumpet wobbly with rain-fuzzed signal, Billie Holiday’s voice curling thin as smoke between drops. Under that, the low, constant thrum of the laundromat’s commercial dryers thrums through the shared wall, a vibration you feel more than hear, rising up through scuffed sneaker soles, punctuated now and then by a muffled clunk of off-balance jeans, a faint beep as soft as a sparrow’s chirp half a block away. In the corner, the old belt-drive turntable spins a scratchy copy of *Blue*, Joni’s voice so quiet you have to lean in to catch the words, the familiar skip on the third verse of “A Case of You” cycling around every three minutes, the belt slipping just enough to warp the note soft for half a second, no one bothering to fix it. Louder than nearly all of it is the rumble of the chonky orange tabby curled on the owner’s lap, purr thick and steady as the dryers, paws kneading slow at the frayed olive corduroy of the armchair, one whisker twitching every time the stove pops and sends a tiny golden spark skittering up the flue.

The stove’s glow gilds the edges of nearby spines, catching the neon foil covers of the half-shelved 1970s sci-fi paperbacks propped against the dented brass cash register, making the hot pink of a tattered Ray Bradbury collection and electric blue of a dog-eared *Dune* flash bright for half a second when the flame licks higher. Half the foil on the Bradbury is peeled back, stuck to the bottom of the stack from a root beer spill last July; the *Dune* bears a faded coffee ring blotted into its cover, left by someone who set their mug down mid-chapter in 1978 and never wiped it up. The owner meant to shelve them three days ago, then got lost reading a passage about frozen methane oceans and left them there, no rush to move them.

On the outside of the front window, a single crimson maple leaf is stuck flat to the glass, edges curled brown where two days of rain have soaked through. Droplets track slow, meandering paths down the fogged pane, cutting clear rivulets through the mist; one cuts right across the lopsided ghost a seven-year-old drew with a chubby finger that morning, smudging its wobbly smile so it grins crookedly out at the rain. Down behind the bottom shelf of 20th century poetry, a tiny deer mouse peeks out, fur soft as dandelion down, black button eyes glinting, nose twitching as it creeps slow across the baseboard to nibble the crumb of pumpkin bread the owner dropped at mid-morning. It holds the crumb in delicate tiny front paws, nibbling so quiet you can’t hear it over the rain, darting back behind the shelf when a gust rattles the pane a little harder. The owner knows it’s there, leaves extra crumbs most days, doesn’t set traps—says any creature that hangs around the Mary Oliver shelf pays its rent.

By the door, a chipped 1998 Powell’s mug sits full of chewed pencil stubs, most of them yellow Dixon Ticonderogas, one with deep cat-tooth marks sunk into its pink eraser, jumbled next to free rubber stamps: one shaped exactly like the orange tabby, one spotted red-capped mushroom, one wobbly tiny ghost, one five-pointed star, ink pads in forest green, cherry red, and matte black tucked under the mug’s base. Next to it, the stack of thrifted knit blankets is folded without care for straight edges: a cream one dotted with old coffee stains, a forest green one with half-frayed tassels, a lumpy hand-knit gray one the owner’s daughter left last Christmas, saying it smelled too much like old paper and wood smoke to take back to her new, paint-fumed Seattle apartment.

Pull any random book off an eye-level shelf, and there’s a nine-in-ten chance of a scribble in the margin, none of them profound: next to a *Leaves of Grass* passage about the open road, “ate the best peach of my life here 8/12/09”; in a tattered Le Guin novel, “my ex left this, he was bad at kissing but had great taste in books”; next to a Mary Oliver poem about wild geese, a teen’s 2017 sparkly-purple scrawl: “this made me cry in the lunch bathroom”; in a beat-up hiking guide, tiny slug doodles next to every trail entry. The half-mug of spiced cider on the scuffed side table has gone lukewarm, a single clove stuck to its rim, a cinnamon stick half-submerged. The half-eaten snickerdoodle rests on a crumpled napkin beside it, a dusting of cinnamon sugar smudged on the table edge where the cat stepped across it before curling up. The owner’s glasses slip down his nose, his hand resting light on the cat’s orange back, rising and falling slow with each purr, not quite asleep, not quite awake, not counting the minutes as they drift soft as rain, soft as paper pages, soft as smoke curling up the flue. (Word count: 887)

The grain of the oak catches the thin fur on my belly right where the varnish wore thin, right where I curl every day, rough but not scratchy, familiar as the shape of my own paws. Sun sits heavy on the tabby patch on my shoulder, the one the color of dry wheat by the fence, warm enough to sink into, thick, like someone laid a soft warm paw right there and isn’t going to move it.

Clover smell drifts through the screen slow, honey-thick, same as the sticky stuff I licked off the counter last month that made my paw stick to my face for three whole minutes while I groomed it off, sweet, not the sharp fake sweet of the crinkly candy wrapper I chewed once that made my tongue tingle bad.

My front left paw pad still holds the heat from the concrete by the peony bush, the spot I curled on an hour ago when a cloud passed over, the concrete held the sun even when the sky went gray, that heat is seeping slow up my leg now, all the way to that matted tuft of fur on my ankle I always forget to lick smooth. There’s a little grit of garden dirt between two toes, I can feel it, don’t care enough to wiggle my paw to dislodge it.

Tinny tinkle far off, three blocks over, the thing that makes the small humans scream and run down the sidewalk. Not a dog bark, not a vacuum, not the doorbell, so it doesn’t matter. Fades, comes back soft, fades again.

White fluff bobs past the glass, slow, dandelion, the stuff that explodes into a hundred floaty bits when you bat it. I track it with half an eye, don’t move my head. Chased one once all the way across the yard, ran face first into the fence post, ear stung for two minutes, person made that soft high noise and scratched under my chin. Too warm to chase this one. It bobs up, bobs down, gone over the neighbor’s shed roof.

Memory of this morning drifts, fuzzy, no edges: the crinkly wand, blue feather on the end, person wiggling it by the couch, I ran so fast my paws slid on the hardwood, jumped three feet straight up, bit the feather so hard a little tuft came off, left the whole wand under the couch next to the dust bunny as big as my head that I batted around for ten minutes before I got tired. My muscles are loose now, soft, like when I stretch so long my toes curl all the way out, no tightness, no urge to run.

Bzzzt. Something hits the screen right by my nose, hard enough to make the mesh hum. One whisker twitches, that’s all. Fuzzy black and yellow, bumblebee, the slow ones that roll around in the lavender blooms too busy to sting. It buzzes louder for a second, bumps the screen again, then the sound drifts off, toward the clover patch probably. Good.

Tuna thought drifts in soft, no hurry, no hunger pang yet, just certainty. The extra creamy kind, the tin that crinkles loud when person peels the lid back, the one that smells so rich my tail tip twitches all on its own even half asleep. They always give me extra, no need to do the stupid sit trick, no need to let the loud small neighbor kid pet my fur the wrong way first, just the cool ceramic dish set down on the mat by the fridge, glistening pink, extra juice to lap up after. It’s coming. Don’t have to beg. Don’t have to remind them. It’s as sure as the sun on my shoulder.

Sparrow hops on the fence, little brown one, pecking at a sunflower seed that fell from the bird feeder. I don’t chatter at it. Too warm. My tail twitches once, slow, the tip brushing the scratch I put in the sill last month when thunder boomed so loud I dug my claws in hard, person didn’t even yell, just picked me up and held me until the thunder stopped. The sparrow flits off to the maple tree. Gone.

Sun shifts a little, moves up to the thin-furred spot at the base of my ear, warm right on the skin. Wind picks up just enough to ruffle the fur on the top of my head, carries cut grass smell now, neighbor mowed their lawn an hour ago, the sharp green smell is faded soft now, mixes with the clover. I can hear person in the kitchen, clink of a glass, they’re making that leaf-smelling tea they drink, the one they held down for me to sniff once before it got too hot. Don’t have to get up to check on them. They’re there. They’ll be there when I decide to move.

Tiny huff of breath out my nose stirs a loose tabby hair on the sill in front of my face, it skitters half an inch, stops. Don’t bat at it. Too much effort.

The ice cream truck tinkle is gone entirely now, too far to hear. The dandelion fluff is long gone. The bee is long gone. The sparrow is long gone. My tail tip hangs over the edge of the sill, I can feel the cool inside air on it, don’t bother tucking it up. There’s a cobweb in the window corner, I watched the spider spin it three nights ago, haven’t batted it down yet, two gnats stuck in the strands, one tiny spider leg peeking out of the crack in the wood where it hides. It’s their web. They can have it.

Thin cloud drifts over the sun for two seconds, the light goes soft, dim, then the sun comes back, just as warm. My whiskers feel heavy, drooping a little. I lick my lips once, slow, rough tongue, catch a little bit of the grass and clover taste on the air. Too much effort to lick again. Too much effort to do anything. The wood under me smells like old varnish and sun and my own fur, the smell that means I don’t have to go anywhere, I don’t have to do anything, no wands to chase, no strange noises to run from, no laps to sit on unless I feel like it later when the sun moves off the sill.

Wait, was that the crinkle of a tuna tin? No, just the screen shifting in the wind. Too early anyway. That’s fine. Time moves slow here. My heart beats slow, thump thump, matching the drift of the clouds, slow, slow. A gnat lands on my paw, I don’t shake it off. It crawls a little, then flies away. The sun is the perfect temperature. Not so hot I have to shift to the shade patch by the curtain, not so cool I have to tuck all my paws under my chest and curl tighter. Perfect.

A ladybug crawls along the window frame, red with black spots, moving slower than I am. I let my eyes slip almost all the way shut, just a thin slit of light coming through, enough to see the bright red dot crawl, crawl, crawl, until it hits the edge of the frame and turns around. The clover smell gets a little sweeter. Somewhere a screen door slams soft, far away. Doesn’t matter. My breath goes slower, slower. The heat on my shoulder seeps all the way down to my bones. I don’t remember what I was going to think about next. Doesn’t matter.
