dream_response:
The rusted screen door on the cabin closest to the general store has a lopsided toad-shaped patch stitched into its mesh, fixed there 18 years prior when a bear cub swiped at a bumblebee tangled in the wire. Through its gaps curls the sharp-sweet tang of pine resin tangled up with simmering apple butter, the batch stirred that morning by a retired forest witch who dropped a handful of crushed white pine needles into the cast iron pot an hour in and decided not to fish them out. A single aspen leaf, edged in the first flush of butter-yellow, sticks to the screen for three slow heartbeats before a breeze tugs it free to spin down the packed-dirt sidewalk.

Shallow enough that smooth, water-worn cobbles poke up above its surface in rounded humps, the creek glints where slanted afternoon sun slants through the tree canopy, flecks of light skittering across the current like scattered silver no one’s in a rush to collect. Caddisfly cases cling to the undersides of half-submerged rocks, rough little bundles of twig and sand, and water striders skate across sun-dappled patches without leaving a ripple that lasts longer than a breath. The aspen leaf that tugged free of the screen door drifts down to settle on the water, floating slow toward the beaver pond half a mile downstream, no current fast enough to jostle it.

The chonky orange tabby everyone calls Tubs—seventeen pounds, known for sneaking beef jerky sticks off the checkout rack when the owner’s back is turned—lies curled tight around the glass jar of free wildflower honey sticks on the store counter, his purr so deep and steady it makes the jar rattle against the worn pine wood. He doesn’t even like honey; he just likes the way the glass holds the sun’s warmth long after the countertop cools in the creeping afternoon shade, one paw slung loose over the jar lid like he’s posted guard. A small child with popsicle stickiness crusted at the corner of their mouth creeps up, carefully lifts his paw half an inch to tug free a blackberry-flavored honey stick, and sets his paw back down like he never noticed a thing. He blinks one slow, gold eye and doesn’t move.

Three houses up, on a porch with gray weathered boards splintered at the edges, a retired witch sits on a splintered wooden bench beside a chipped ceramic mug of spiced cider, a heap of long, soft ponderosa pine needles piled at her feet. A cluster of grubby seven-year-olds circles her, jeans crusted with grass stains, one sporting a knee scab crusted over with pine sap, as she shows them how to twist the needles tight, tuck the raw ends in so they don’t poke delicate wrist skin. The finished bracelets hold the faint, cool smell of summer rain, the kind that rolls through fast at dusk in mid-July and leaves the ferns glistening for hours after. One of the kids tucks a fluffy gone-to-seed dandelion behind her ear, and she doesn’t brush it off.

Wobbly, unpolished, the sound of a new fiddle player drifts down from a cabin half a mile up the hillside, the player fumbling the same four-bar stretch of an old folk tune every third pass, slowing, resetting, trying again, getting it a little smoother each time. The sound bounces off pine trunks, tangles in aspen branches, drifts down to the general store porch where two long-time residents sit on split-log stools passing a mason jar of spiced cider between them, barely talking. One taps the scuffed toe of his work boot in time even when the player flubs a note so bad the string twangs sharp, nodding like that’s exactly how the tune is meant to sound on a Tuesday in late September.

An hour before sunset, the first thin curl of woodsmoke lifts from the chimney of the cabin at the edge of town where the wooden spoon carver lives, who lit his evening fire early when the air turned sharp enough to pinken the knuckles of anyone out longer than ten minutes. He’s burning aspen logs split back in May, cured all summer, so the smoke smells sweet and light as it curls up into the sky that’s already softening from bright high-alpine blue to hazy lavender at the horizon. The tang of fresh-pressed cider from the press set up outside the post office mixes with the smoke, sharp and bright on the back of your throat when you breathe in deep.

A hiker in too-big scuffed hiking boots, flannel tied around their waist, trips over a raised gnarled root stepping off the post office curb, and the paper bag of warm cinnamon rolls they just bought from the pop-up stand spills open across the patch of white clover growing along the sidewalk. They stand there for a beat, hands on their hips, laughing hard enough their shoulders shake, before they even bend to start picking them up, and that’s when the small local herd of cow elk ambles through town—three cows, two wobbly calves still fuzzy with their first winter coat coming in. They pause, tilt their soft dark eyes at the rolls, lean down to crunch a few right there in the clover, powdered sugar and cream cheese icing sticking to the fur around their noses, before the lead cow flicks her ear and leads the rest up the trail toward the high meadows, leaving half a squished roll for the squirrels. The hiker walks back to the pop-up stand, buys a second bag, and holds it tight to their chest this time.

The one-room town library has shelves crammed so full of books stacks teeter on the floor, its windows fogged at the edges from the pot of masala chai simmering on the little space heater by the front door. The long-haired gray library cat everyone calls Dust Bunny—for the permanent fine layer of book lint dusting her fur—jumps up on the arm of the overstuffed corduroy armchair by the window, where a part-time trail maintenance worker who moved to town eight months ago for the lack of cell service is napping, head tilted back, mouth slightly open, a half-read field guide to local mushrooms splayed across his chest. She bats once at the stack of 1970s poetry collections teetering on the armrest—Mary Oliver, Gary Snyder, a tattered anthology no one has checked out since 1982—and the whole stack topples soft as thistledown onto his lap. He snorts awake, blinks blearily, lifts her up to settle on his shoulder, tugs the frayed wool throw tighter over his legs, and falls right back to sleep, the books still spread across his thighs. She curls into the crook of his neck, purring, and bats a mushroom-shaped paper bookmark off the arm to flutter to the floor.

On the post office porch, a wicker basket with a gingham-wrapped handle sits piled so high with zucchini some are as long and thick as a toddler’s arm, a sign scrawled in sparkly purple marker propped against the pile: take as many as you want, i am begging you, i can’t make any more zucchini bread, my freezer is full, my chickens won’t even eat them anymore. A retired witch on her way to check her PO box tucks two small, tender zucchinis into her canvas tote and leaves a half-pint jar of wild blackberry jam in the empty spot as a trade. A teenager skidding by on a beat-up skateboard with squeaky wheels grabs one of the giant zucchinis, tucks it under his arm, yells “thanks! pirate sword!” over his shoulder, and keeps rolling, no one calling after him, no one caring.

Up on the grassy hill behind the closed-for-the-season elementary school, a group of teenagers drags four dusty old rubber tire tubes up to the crest, dragged out of a garage where they sat all summer, even though the first snow is still two months off at least. They take turns flopping belly-down on the tubes and rolling down, whooping so loud the sound carries all the way to the creek, jackets flapping, one veering off course to roll straight into a patch of purple wild asters, coming up with petals stuck in their hair and grass down the back of their shirt, laughing so hard they can’t stand up for a full minute. The town’s unofficial golden retriever—no fixed address, fed by everyone, free to wander where he likes—runs up and down the slope alongside them, barking soft, tail wagging so hard his whole hind end wiggles, like he’s been appointed official race referee.

The fiddle player up the hill finally nails that tricky four-bar stretch three times in a row, and launches into the next verse, which is even wobblier, full of missed notes and pauses while they fumble for finger placement. The breeze picks up, spinning a handful of aspen leaves loose from their branches to twirl slow to the ground, one landing right on the lid of Tubs’ honey jar; he twitches one ear but doesn’t wake. The faint rain-scent from the pine needle bracelets catches the wind, drifts down to the creek, where the floating aspen leaf bobs past a rock where a chipmunk sits stuffing its cheeks full of sunflower seeds left out by the general store owner. The lead elk pauses halfway up the trail, turns to look back at the town, icing still crusted on her nose, before she steps into the treeline and out of sight.

The teenager with the zucchini sword stops at the stop sign at the end of the main road, dueling it for a minute, the vegetable making a soft thwack sound against the metal every time he swings. The two old timers on the general store porch pass a jar of pickled beets back and forth, no words exchanged, just one holding it out, the other taking a crisp spear, passing it back. A screen door slams soft somewhere down the road, not loud enough to startle the nuthatch hopping along the power line. Tubs stretches slow on the counter, all four legs extended, claws poking out to knead the worn wood, and a honey stick rolls off the edge to clatter on the floor, rolling under the shelf where they stock pine-scented beeswax candles, and no one bends down to pick it up right now. The sun dips a little lower, gilding the edge of every aspen leaf on the hillside until the whole slope glows like it’s dusted with faint, soft gold, and the air turns just cold enough that you can see your breath if you huff out slow. A ladybug crawls across the sparkly purple sign on the zucchini basket, making its slow way across the word “begging,” before it spreads its tiny red wings and flies off toward the stand of old pines at the edge of town.
